n: The tribes descended from Joseph receive the central hill country, the heart of the land. Their southern border begins at the Jordan near Jericho and climbs toward Bethel.

f.g: The spring at Jericho, today called Elisha’s Spring.

n: The line runs past Bethel and Luz. Bethel is where Jacob saw the ladder to heaven; Luz was its older name or a neighboring town.

f.g: The home clan of Hushai the Archite, David’s friend.

n: The border goes down the western slopes past Lower Beth-horon and Gezer to the Mediterranean.

f.g: In KJV English “coast” usually means border or territory, not seashore.

n: Joseph’s two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh, each became a full tribe, so Joseph received a double portion — the birthright blessing.
Now Ephraim’s own borders are traced. Its land ran from the Bethel area north to about Shechem.

f.g: Upper Beth-horon, on the ridge above the valley of Aijalon.

n: The northern edge runs from Michmethah, near Shechem, east toward the Jordan valley.

f.g: A site southeast of Shechem; not the city of Shiloh itself.

n: The eastern line drops down into the Jordan valley near Jericho, closing the outline of Ephraim.

f.g: “Crowns”; a common town name in the region.

n: On the west, the brook Kanah separates Ephraim from Manasseh as it flows to the sea.

f.g: Probably the Wadi Qanah, a seasonal stream flowing west into the Yarkon.

n: Some Ephraimite towns lay inside Manasseh’s area. The brother tribes’ land was interwoven, as their history would be.

f.g: Towns set apart for Ephraim though located in Manasseh’s territory.

n: Ephraim left the Canaanites in Gezer and made them pay forced labor instead. This half-obedience becomes a pattern that Judges shows bearing bitter fruit.

f.g: Were made to do forced labor or pay tribute.
